Central stellar temperature (Tc​=T(0))

Words: 32
Stellar structure OurBigBook.com
The temperature at a star's centre. In gas-pressure-supported stellar homology, the stellar hydrostatic equation and ideal gas law give Tc​∝μGM/(RR), with a coefficient set by the dimensionless density and pressure profiles. It controls the strongly temperature-dependent stellar energy-generation rate.

Stellar core (Mc​=m(Rc​))

Words: 77
Stellar structure OurBigBook.com
A stellar core is the central region distinguished from the surrounding envelope by its composition, energy generation or thermodynamic state. A core boundary at radius Rc​ encloses mass Mc​=m(Rc​)=4π∫0Rc​​ρ(r)r2dr. In a hydrogen-shell-burning red giant, a helium-rich core can be inert while a narrow surrounding layer supplies the luminosity. Core mass and core radius are separate variables: the relation between them must come from a structural model, such as a polytropic mass-radius relation, rather than from the word core alone.

Uniformly rotating stellar hydrostatic equilibrium (∇P=−ρ∇ϕ, ∇2ϕ=4πGρ−2Ω2)

Words: 492 Articles: 8
Stellar structure OurBigBook.com
Uniform solid-body rotation adds the centrifugal potential −Ω2ϖ2/2 to the gravitational potential. In the corotating frame, hydrostatic equilibrium becomes ∇P=−ρ∇ϕ. The Poisson equation gives ∇2ϕ=4πGρ−2Ω2. On regular connected equipotential surfaces, P is constant; taking the curl shows that ρ is constant too. Uniform composition and an invertible equation of state then make T constant on each such surface. These statements do not require ∣∇ϕ∣ to be constant there.

Roche model of a uniformly rotating star (ϕ=−GM/r−Ω2ϖ2/2)

Words: 67
Uniformly rotating stellar hydrostatic equilibrium OurBigBook.com
This approximation represents the gravitational potential by a central point mass while retaining the centrifugal potential. A surface through polar radius Rp​ satisfies Rp​/r+q(r/Rp​)2sin2θ/2=1, where q=Ω2Rp3​/(GM). The inner closed surface is regular below q=8/27; at the limiting value its equatorial radius is 3Rp​/2 and equatorial effective gravity vanishes. The approximation is useful for illustrating oblateness and gravity darkening, rather than modeling the density distribution of every rotating star.

Radiative gradient in a uniformly rotating star (∇rad​=16πacGmT43κPL​(1−2πGmΩ2V​)−1)

Words: 50
Uniformly rotating stellar hydrostatic equilibrium OurBigBook.com
The divergence theorem and Poisson equation give ∫S​∇ϕ⋅dS=4πGm−2Ω2V on a bounding equipotential surface. Equipotential luminosity conservation with stellar circulation then fixes f=L/(4πGm−2Ω2V). Combining dT/dϕ=−f/χ, dP/dϕ=−ρ and radiative conductivity gives the displayed logarithmic temperature-pressure gradient. Both appearances of mass mean the enclosed mass m; only on the outer boundary can both be replaced by the total mass.

Meridional circulation in a star

Words: 163 Articles: 2
Uniformly rotating stellar hydrostatic equilibrium OurBigBook.com
Slow circulation in planes containing the rotation axis can transport entropy through a rotating star while the leading mechanical balance remains nearly hydrostatic equilibrium. Its steady mass flux satisfies the continuity equation. It is distinct from assuming an exactly motionless radiative interior, and from turbulent convection.

Eddington-Sweet circulation (tES​∼tKH​GM/(Ω2R3))

Words: 62
Meridional circulation in a star OurBigBook.com
The thermal imbalance of a slowly rotating radiative star can drive stellar meridional circulation. Its fractional centrifugal distortion is ϵΩ​∼Ω2R3/(GM), so balancing an order-ϵΩ​ fraction of the luminosity by thermal advection estimates tES​∼tKH​/ϵΩ​, where tKH​∼GM2/(RL). Stable composition gradients can further impede the circulation. This radiative thermal estimate is different from rapid torque-driven circulation in a convective envelope.

Equipotential luminosity conservation with stellar circulation (∫S​F⋅dS=∫V​ρϵdV)

Words: 57
Meridional circulation in a star OurBigBook.com
For steady stellar meridional circulation, T∇s=∇(h+ϕ) and ∇⋅(ρv)=0. Thus ρv⋅T∇s=∇⋅[ρv(h+ϕ)]. In the leading uniformly rotating stellar hydrostatic equilibrium, h+ϕ is constant on an equipotential surface; its total advected flux vanishes because the net mass flux vanishes. Integrating the energy equation then identifies the outward luminosity with enclosed nuclear energy generation, even though local heat advection is nonzero.

Radiative-equilibrium obstruction in a rotating barotropic star (∇⋅(f∇ϕ)=f′∣∇ϕ∣2+f∇2ϕ)

Words: 46
Uniformly rotating stellar hydrostatic equilibrium OurBigBook.com
On a regular equipotential surface, f,f′,ρ and ∇2ϕ are constant, but ∣∇ϕ∣2 generally varies. Consequently a flux F=f(ϕ)∇ϕ cannot ordinarily satisfy local radiative equilibrium ∇⋅F=ρϵ at all latitudes. Special cases such as f′=0 or spherical symmetry evade this obstruction. Stellar meridional circulation supplies heat advection in the leading hydrostatic treatment.

Gravity darkening

Words: 103 Articles: 1
Uniformly rotating stellar hydrostatic equilibrium OurBigBook.com
Gravity darkening is the variation of surface brightness and effective temperature with effective gravity over a rotating or tidally distorted star. Lower equatorial gravity generally corresponds to cooler equatorial regions. The radiative gravity-darkening law applies to the idealized uniformly rotating, radiatively transporting, composition-uniform case; its exponent is not universal for every stellar envelope.

Radiative gravity-darkening law (Fn​∝g, Te​∝g1/4)

Words: 57
Gravity darkening OurBigBook.com
In uniformly rotating stellar hydrostatic equilibrium, composition-uniform thermodynamic quantities are functions of the total potential. Radiative conductivity gives F=f(ϕ)∇ϕ, with f=−χdT/dϕ. On one surface, f is constant, so the outward flux is Fn​=fg. The Stefan–Boltzmann law therefore gives Te​∝g1/4. This is a surface-flux law: the material temperature constant on an interior equipotential is not the latitude-dependent emergent effective temperature.

Uniform-density stellar model (ρ=3M/(4πR3))

Words: 38
Stellar structure OurBigBook.com
A uniform-density spherical hydrostatic equilibrium model with zero surface pressure has P(r)=2πGρ2(R2−r2)/3, M=4πρR3/3 and gravitational energy −3GM2/(5R). A perfect gas can have this mechanical structure with varying temperature and entropy; the imposed equilibrium density does not require incompressible perturbations.

Linear-density stellar model (ρ(r)=ρc​(1−r/R))

Words: 55
Stellar structure OurBigBook.com
An imposed spherical profile ρ=ρc​(1−r/R) gives M=πρc​R3/3 in hydrostatic equilibrium. For an ideal gas with zero surface pressure, P=Pc​(1−x)2(1+2x−9x2/5) and T=Tc​(1−x)(1+2x−9x2/5), where x=r/R, Pc​=5GM2/(4πR4) and Tc​=5GM/(12RR). The density has a central cusp and temperature initially rises outward, so positive outward radiative diffusion with regular positive nuclear heating cannot satisfy this imposed profile near the centre.

Stellar energy balance equation (∂L/∂m=ϵnuc​−ϵν​−Du/Dt−PD(1/ρ)/Dt)

Words: 151 Articles: 2
Stellar structure OurBigBook.com
For a slowly evolving spherical star, the Lagrangian energy equation separates nuclear rest-mass release, stellar neutrino energy loss, thermal storage and pressure-volume work. Specific internal energy and nuclear energy conventions must avoid counting nuclear mass changes or escaping reaction-neutrino energy twice. At fixed composition the gravothermal stellar energy generation is −TDS/Dt. Energy transport processes redistribute heat rather than creating it.

Stellar neutrino energy loss (ϵν​≥0)

Words: 47
Stellar energy balance equation OurBigBook.com
Escaping neutrinos remove energy produced by nuclear reactions or drawn from thermal reservoirs. Pair annihilation, plasma excitations, photoneutrino emission and electron-ion bremsstrahlung provide thermal losses. This reduces photon luminosity or increases the required nuclear and gravothermal supply. At sufficiently extreme collapse densities, neutrino transport must replace a free-escape loss approximation.

Gravothermal stellar energy generation (ϵgrav​=−Du/Dt−PD(1/ρ)/Dt)

Words: 50
Stellar energy balance equation OurBigBook.com
This term accounts for thermal storage and compression or expansion in the stellar energy balance equation. At fixed composition the first law of thermodynamics makes it −TDS/Dt. Kelvin-Helmholtz contraction can supply positive luminosity, while thermal adjustment may locally absorb energy. It is not simply the full change in gravitational potential energy: the stellar virial theorem also requires changes in internal energy.

Stellar gas-pressure fraction (β=Pgas​/(Pgas​+Prad​))

Words: 104 Articles: 1
Stellar structure OurBigBook.com
The gas-pressure fraction describes the relative support by an ideal gas and radiation pressure. For monatomic gas plus equilibrium radiation, it determines the adiabatic exponents of a monatomic gas-radiation mixture. Its value at the unperturbed state may be specified, but it generally changes during an isentropic parcel displacement.

Uniform gas-pressure fraction and constant-luminosity radiative-envelope incompatibility (β,κ constant ⟹ Lr​/m=4πcG(1−β)/κ)

Words: 65
Stellar gas-pressure fraction OurBigBook.com
For a radiative envelope, dPrad​/dP=κLr​/(4πcGm). Exactly uniform stellar gas-pressure fraction instead requires this derivative to be 1−β. Constant opacity therefore requires Lr​ to increase in proportion to enclosed mass. A positive-density finite-mass envelope with no local energy generation has constant Lr​ and cannot satisfy all these conditions pointwise. The Eddington-model convective-core mass fraction uses constant β as a global approximation, rather than an exact detailed envelope constraint.

Stellar thermal equilibrium (Lsurface​=Lheat​−Lν​)

Words: 90
Stellar structure OurBigBook.com
In stellar structure, stellar thermal equilibrium means that internal heating balances the surface luminosity and any energy loss through neutrinos, with negligible secular storage of thermal energy on the timescale considered. A star can satisfy this balance while its interior is hotter than its surface and heat flows outward. It is therefore different from equal-temperature thermal equilibrium between systems. Neglecting neutrino losses, the balance is Lsurface​=Lheat​. In a slowly mass-losing donor star, a stellar thermal equilibrium radius sequence applies only when thermal adjustment is fast compared with the mass-loss timescale; rapid loss instead requires the adiabatic stellar radius response exponent.

Stellar equation-of-state regime diagram

Words: 286 Articles: 4
Stellar structure OurBigBook.com
A temperature versus density diagram separates classical, degenerate, nonrelativistic and relativistic stellar-matter limits. The Electron degeneracy boundary is T∼TF​(ρ), with slope 2/3 at low density and 1/3 at high density. Thermal relativity is controlled by kB​T∼me​c2, while relativity of degenerate Electrons is controlled by pF​∼me​c. Photon pressure and thermal electron-positron pairs add further crossovers; all depend on composition and are gradual, not thermodynamic phase boundaries.

Ionic Coulomb coupling parameter (Γ=Z2e2/(4πϵ0​ai​kB​T))

Words: 85
Stellar equation-of-state regime diagram OurBigBook.com
For one ionic species of number density ni​, the ion-sphere radius is ai​=(3/(4πni​))1/3. The ionic Coulomb coupling parameter compares the interaction energy from Coulomb's law at that separation with thermal energy kB​T. At fixed composition, Γ∝ρ1/3/T. Values near one mark significant corrections to the ideal ion gas; strong coupling can lead to an ordered solid. Screening, mixtures and quantum motion modify detailed transitions, so this estimate is not a universal crystallization boundary. It is separate from the electron degeneracy criterion based on the electron Fermi temperature.

Radiation-to-degeneracy pressure boundary

Words: 55
Stellar equation-of-state regime diagram OurBigBook.com
Equating radiation pressure to cold electron degeneracy pressure gives T=[3Pe​(ρ)/arad​]1/4. Because the two Electron pressure limits scale as ρ5/3 and ρ4/3, this boundary has logarithmic slopes 5/12 and 1/3, respectively. Above it, photon pressure can dominate even when the net Electrons remain degenerate; degeneracy of one component and dominance of the total pressure are different criteria. Thermal pairs modify the high-temperature pressure comparison.

Radiation-to-gas pressure boundary

Words: 38
Stellar equation-of-state regime diagram OurBigBook.com
For a nondegenerate fully ionized gas, equating Pgas​=ρkB​T/(μmol​mu​) with Pγ​=arad​T4/3 gives T3=3kB​ρ/(arad​μmol​mu​). Radiation dominates at higher temperature for fixed density. A degenerate Electron gas requires its degeneracy pressure instead of extrapolating this ideal-gas formula.

Thermal electron relativistic threshold (T∗​=me​c2/kB​)

Words: 42
Stellar equation-of-state regime diagram OurBigBook.com
In a dilute Electron gas, thermal kinetic energies become relativistic near kB​T=me​c2, corresponding to T∗​≃5.93×109K. This is a crossover in the momentum distribution, not an abrupt temperature transition. Degenerate Electrons can instead be relativistic at much lower temperature if their Fermi momentum exceeds me​c.

Stellar composition profile

Words: 32
Stellar structure OurBigBook.com
A stellar composition profile gives chemical mass fractions against radius or enclosed mass. Flat portions can indicate mixing in a convective core or convective envelope, while burning shells and moving convective boundaries leave gradients and discontinuities.

Stellar structure equations

Stellar structure OurBigBook.com
The stellar structure equations describe spherical hydrostatic stars through radial conservation of mass, force balance, energy generation, and energy transport. An equation of state, opacity, energy-generation law, and boundary conditions close the system.

Stellar structure equations OurBigBook.com
In spherical stellar structure, a shell of radius r, thickness dr and mass density ρ has mass dm=4πr2ρdr. Integrating outward gives the enclosed mass, m(r)=4π∫0r​ρ(s)s2ds.

Adiabatic exponents of a monatomic gas-radiation mixture (Γ1​=(32−24β−3β2)/(24−21β))

Words: 99 Articles: 1
Stellar adiabatic exponent OurBigBook.com
For fixed-composition monatomic ideal gas plus equilibrium radiation pressure, specific internal energy is u=3RT/2+ar​T4/ρ. An isentropic process satisfies du=Pdρ/ρ2, giving Γ3​−1=(8−6β)/(24−21β) and
Γ2​=24−18β−3β232−24β−3β2​,∇ad​=32−24β−3β28−6β​.
(2)
The stellar gas-pressure fraction must be allowed to change along the adiabat. The pure-radiation and pure-gas limits give Γ1​=Γ2​=4/3 and 5/3, respectively. Partial ionization or different gas heat capacities change these formulas.

Specific heats of a monatomic gas-radiation mixture (cP​=R(32−24β−3β2)/(2β2))

Adiabatic exponents of a monatomic gas-radiation mixture OurBigBook.com
For fixed-composition monatomic ideal gas plus equilibrium blackbody radiation, let R=k/(μH) and β=Pg​/P. The mass-specific heats are cP​=R(32−24β−3β2)/(2β2) and cV​=R(24−21β)/(2β). The specific-heat ratio is Γ1​/β, not generally any one of the stellar adiabatic exponents. Differentiate at constant total pressure rather than at constant β.

Stellar polytrope

Words: 845 Articles: 19
Stellar structure OurBigBook.com
A stellar polytrope obeys P=Kρ1+1/n for constant K and polytropic index n. Its dimensionless density profile satisfies the Lane-Emden equation.

Polytrope of index five (θ=(1+ξ2/3)−1/2)

Words: 88 Articles: 1
Stellar polytrope OurBigBook.com
The regular n=5 Lane-Emden equation solution has no finite first zero. Its Lane-Emden mass formula gives m(ξ)=4πρc​α3ξ3/[3(1+ξ2/3)3/2], so its infinite-radius total mass is 4π3​ρc​α3. Its enclosed mean mass density is ρc​(1+ξ2/3)−3/2 and tends to zero. A finite externally confined core instead requires a specified truncation pressure.

Luminosity integral of an index-five polytrope (L=12π3​ϵ0​α3ρc2​Tcq​∫01​u2(1−u2)(q+5)/2du)

Words: 48
Polytrope of index five OurBigBook.com
For a gas-pressure-supported polytrope of index five with uniform mean molecular weight, T/Tc​=θ. A specific stellar energy-generation rate ϵ=ϵ0​ρTq therefore integrates to 4πϵ0​α3ρc2​Tcq​∫0∞​ξ2θ10+qdξ. Substituting u=ξ/3+ξ2​ gives the displayed formula, convergent for q>−7. At q=11 its dimensionless coefficient is approximately 1.02942. The scale factor is a volume, α3, rather than an area.

Moment of inertia of a polytropic star (I/(MR2))

Words: 58
Stellar polytrope OurBigBook.com
For a spherical stellar polytrope, the axial moment of inertia is I=(8π/3)∫0R​ρ(r)r4dr. With Lane-Emden variables for a stellar polytrope, first zero ξ1​ and Lane-Emden surface mass constant ωn​, its dimensionless form is
MR2I​=3ωn​ξ12​2​∫0ξ1​​ξ4θ(ξ)ndξ.
(5)
A polytrope of index zero gives 2/5, while a polytrope of index one gives (2/3)(1−6/π2). The latter is smaller because more of the mass lies near the center. The scalar second mass moment ∫r2dm is 3I/2, not the axial moment of inertia.

Polytrope of index zero (θ(ξ)=1−ξ2/6)

Words: 51
Stellar polytrope OurBigBook.com
The regular n=0 solution of the Lane-Emden equation is θ=1−ξ2/6, with first zero 6​. Its interior density is constant and its pressure varies as θ. This is the structural incompressible limit; P=Kρ1+1/n itself is singular at n=0, and does not assign the perturbative stellar adiabatic exponent of a thermally stratified ideal-gas model.

Low-density polytropic mass divergence (M∝ρc(3−n)/(2n)​)

Words: 48
Stellar polytrope OurBigBook.com
For p=Kρ1+1/n, the Lane-Emden mass formula gives M∝ρc(3−n)/(2n)​ at fixed K, while M/R∝ρc1/n​. For 3<n<5, the Lane-Emden equation has a finite-radius solution, yet M→∞ as ρc​→0. The relativistic Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff equation approaches this limit since pc​/ρc​→0. Monotone pressure and density alone therefore do not impose a finite stellar maximum mass.

Gravitational energy of a stellar polytrope (Ω=−3GM2/[(5−n)R])

Words: 49
Stellar polytrope OurBigBook.com
For a spherical stellar polytrope of finite radius and zero surface pressure, the specific enthalpy is (n+1)P/ρ. Hydrostatic equilibrium gives h+Φ=−GM/R, hence (n+1)∫PdV=−GM2/R−2Ω. Eliminating the pressure integral with the stellar virial theorem proves the displayed formula. For a gas adiabatic stellar polytrope, n=1/(γ−1) and U=GM2/[(5γ−6)R]; a general polytropic index need not have this relation to the specific-heat ratio.

Polytrope of index one (P=Kρ2)

Words: 251 Articles: 3
Stellar polytrope OurBigBook.com
A stellar polytrope with polytropic index one has ∇Φ=−2K∇ρ in hydrostatic equilibrium. Combining this with the Poisson equation for Newtonian gravity gives the Helmholtz equation
∇2ρ+k2ρ=0,k2=K2πG​.
(8)
The spherical solution regular at the origin is ρ(r)=ρc​sin(kr)/(kr). Its first zero gives R=π/k=πK/(2G)​, independent of central mass density, and ρˉ​/ρc​=3/π2.

The radiative-zero choice T0​=0 is exact for a vanishing-temperature boundary at infinity and a deep-envelope approximation for a very extended finite star. It is not implied by small surface temperature alone at a specified finite radius.

Self-gravitating Kramers power-law envelope

Words: 81
Radiative envelope OurBigBook.com
For a constant-luminosity radiative envelope with ideal-gas pressure and Kramers' opacity law, impose power laws on enclosed mass, density, pressure and temperature while retaining Mr′​=4πr2ρ. If their exponents are m,b,p,d, respectively, mass conservation gives m=b+3, hydrostatic balance gives d=m−1, the gas law gives d=p−b, and diffusion gives d−1=2b−2−13d/2. Solving gives (m,b,p,d)=(1,−32,−42,−10)/11. In particular R/rc​=(Tc​/TR​)11/10. Neglecting envelope self-gravity instead sets Mr​ approximately constant and changes the exponents to d=−1,b=−13/4,p=−17/4; that approximation is not an exact solution of mass conservation with nonzero density.

Power-law opacity radiative envelope (∇rad​=Pn+1/(CTn+s+4))

Words: 170 Articles: 2
Radiative envelope OurBigBook.com
A thin radiative envelope with constant enclosed mass, luminosity and mean molecular weight, ideal gas pressure and opacity κ=κ0​ρnT−s has a=n+1, b=n+s+4, and C=16πarad​cGM/[3κ0​(μmu​/kB​)nL]. Combining radiative diffusion in a star with hydrostatic equilibrium gives ∇rad​=Pa/(CTb), so Pa−P0a​=(aC/b)(Tb−T0b​) for nonzero exponents. Zero exponents give logarithmic limits. The model must be stopped or modified if the Schwarzschild criterion predicts convection.
Radiative-envelope convection matching (∇rad​(Tb​)=∇ad​)
Words: 119 Articles: 1
Power-law opacity radiative envelope OurBigBook.com
For P=C(Tb+K)1/p with p=n+1 and b=4+n+m, the logarithmic radiative temperature gradient is (p/b)(1+K/Tb). At a marginal boundary with an efficient ideal-gas convective envelope, the Schwarzschild criterion equates it to (γ−1)/γ. Hence K=Tbb​[(b/p)(γ−1)/γ−1]. The notation K=T0b​ with real positive T0​ requires a nonnegative bracket. Vanishing p or b needs the corresponding logarithmic integration instead of this power form.
Deep radiative boundary beneath a power-law-opacity convective envelope (Tb​∝Te−(8β+2)/7​)
Words: 62
Radiative-envelope convection matching OurBigBook.com
In a negligible-mass, non-burning stellar envelope with P=KT5/2 and Kramers' opacity law κ=κ1​ρT−7/2, the stellar radiative temperature gradient is ∇rad​=3κ1​μK2L/(16πacRGMT7/2). It decreases inward as the temperature rises, so the inner edge of efficient convection is where it equals 2/5. If outer matching gives K∝g1/2Te−2β−5/2​, then Tb7/2​∝K2L/M∝Te−4β−1​, since g=GM/R2 and L=4πR2σTe4​. Hence Tb​∝Te−(8β+2)/7​.

Fully convective star

Words: 25
Stellar convective stability OurBigBook.com
A fully convective star has convection throughout nearly its entire interior. Very low-mass red dwarfs are fully convective; the transition to this structure is used in the disrupted magnetic braking model.

Radiative stellar structure

Words: 396 Articles: 10
Stellar structure OurBigBook.com
In a radiative stellar region, photons carry luminosity down the temperature gradient. Dimensional scaling of the radiative-diffusion equation gives L∼RTc4​/(κc​ρc​).

Radiative core

Words: 26
Radiative stellar structure OurBigBook.com
A stellar core in which radiative diffusion in a star carries most of the energy, rather than convection. Its formation in a pre-main-sequence star breaks the fully convective assumption behind an idealized Hayashi track.

Stellar radiative temperature gradient (∇rad​=3κLr​P/(16πar​cGmT4))

Words: 38
Radiative stellar structure OurBigBook.com
The radiative temperature gradient needed to carry a spherical stellar luminosity follows by dividing radiative diffusion in a star by the hydrostatic pressure support equation. It is a logarithmic pressure gradient, not dT/dr itself. Comparing it with the adiabatic temperature gradient by the Schwarzschild criterion determines whether purely radiative transport is locally unstable at uniform composition.

Opacity (κ)

Words: 255 Articles: 5
Radiative stellar structure OurBigBook.com
Opacity is an extinction cross-section per unit mass. It controls the photon mean free path and therefore the radiative temperature gradient in an optically thick star.

Negative hydrogen ion opacity (κ∝ρ1/2T9)

Words: 150 Articles: 1
Opacity OurBigBook.com
The negative hydrogen ion supplies important continuum opacity in cool hydrogen-rich stellar atmospheres. A useful local approximate law is κ=κ0​ρ1/2T9; it is not valid over arbitrary temperatures and compositions. In an ideal gas power-law opacity radiative envelope matched to ∇phot​=1/8, it gives ∇rad​=−1/3+(11/24)(T/Teff​)9/2, rising rapidly toward convective instability.
Negative-hydrogen-opacity alpha-disk thickness scaling (H41/3∼σR6/(κ0​αΩ15Σ7/3))
Words: 107
Negative hydrogen ion opacity OurBigBook.com
Let R=kB​/(μm​mp​) for constant mean molecular weight μm​ in proton-mass units, and let σ be the Stefan–Boltzmann constant in the Stefan–Boltzmann law. The gas sound speed used here satisfies cs2​=RT, and Ω is the local orbital frequency. For the local opacity approximation κ=κ0​ρ1/3T10, a gas-supported optically thick alpha disk has ρ∼Σ/H and RT∼Ω2H2. Integrated viscous heating is F+​∼αΣΩ3H2. Radiative diffusion gives F−​∼(σ/κ0​)T−6Σ−4/3H1/3∼(σ/κ0​)R6Ω−12Σ−4/3H−35/3. Equating the fluxes proves the thickness scaling. At fixed composition and α, it gives H/r∝r53/82Σ−7/41 and cs​∝r6/41Σ−7/41 in Keplerian rotation. Radial powers therefore require a surface-density profile; they are not determined by opacity alone. The formula is local to the stated opacity regime and small disk aspect ratio.

Kramers' opacity law

Words: 17
Opacity OurBigBook.com
The Kramers opacity law has κ=κ0​ρT−7/2 for bound-free and free-free absorption under its idealized ionized-gas assumptions.

Electron-scattering opacity (κes​)

Words: 28
Opacity OurBigBook.com
Electron-scattering opacity is approximately independent of density and temperature in a fully ionized nonrelativistic plasma of fixed composition. For hydrogen mass fraction X, κes​≃0.2(1+X)cm2g−1.

Free-free opacity (κff​)

Words: 34
Opacity OurBigBook.com
Free-free opacity is absorption caused when a photon is absorbed during a Coulomb encounter between an electron and an ion. In the Kramers approximation its Rosseland mean scales approximately as κff​∝ρT−7/2.

Radiative diffusion in a star

Words: 55 Articles: 1
Radiative stellar structure OurBigBook.com
In an optically thick stellar region, radiative diffusion carries luminosity according to
drdT​=−16πarad​cr2T33κρLr​​.
(27)

Radiative conductivity (χ=4acT3/(3κρ))

Words: 38
Radiative diffusion in a star OurBigBook.com
In the optically thick radiative diffusion in a star approximation, the heat flux is F=−χ∇T. The conductivity depends on opacity, mass density and temperature. It relates a material temperature gradient to energy transport and must not be confused with the emergent effective temperature.

Effective temperature (Teff​)

Words: 22
Stellar structure OurBigBook.com
The effective temperature is the temperature of a blackbody with the same radiative flux as a star: L=4πR2σTeff4​.

Mass-luminosity relation

Words: 211 Articles: 4
Stellar structure OurBigBook.com
The mass-luminosity relation connects a star's mass to its luminosity. Its slope depends on opacity, nuclear burning, pressure support, composition, and evolutionary state.

Eddington luminosity (LEdd​)

Words: 188 Articles: 3
Mass-luminosity relation OurBigBook.com
Balancing outward radiative acceleration against gravity gives
LEdd​=κ4πcGM​.
(28)
It is an approximate upper luminosity for a hydrostatic star of opacity κ.

Stellar electron-scattering Eddington factor (Γe​=κe​L/(4πcGM))

Words: 47
Eddington luminosity OurBigBook.com
This factor is the ratio of acceleration due to electron-scattering opacity to gravitational acceleration in a spherical luminous star. The remaining effective gravity is approximately GM(1−Γe​)/R2 when other radiative forces are neglected. Being below the electron-scattering limit does not preclude a line-driven stellar wind, because additional opacity can provide more acceleration.

Dust-grain Eddington limit (LEdd,d​)

Words: 82
Eddington luminosity OurBigBook.com
An isolated compact dust grain of radius rd​ and material density ρd​ has opacity per unit dust mass κd​=3Qpr​/(4ρd​rd​), where Qpr​ is its radiation-pressure efficiency. Its Eddington luminosity is 4πGMc/κd​. Matching the electron-scattering opacity gives rd,crit​=3Qpr​/(4ρd​κes​), approximately 1.9cm for Qpr​=1, ρd​=1gcm−3, and κes​=0.4cm2g−1. At that electron-scattering luminosity, smaller grains feel a net outward force and larger grains remain attracted. This is an isolated-grain force balance, not the opacity of an arbitrary gas-dust mixture.

Radiative force multiplier (M)

Words: 35
Eddington luminosity OurBigBook.com
A radiative force multiplier is the ratio of total radiative acceleration to a reference electron-scattering acceleration. Spectral lines, bound-free absorption, and dust can make M≫1, whereas highly ionized gas approaches M=1.
